newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE - Building boom changes Gulf's facade fast.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Building boom changes Gulf's facade fast.

text.p: Go away for three weeks and foundations of new buildings and shopping malls as well as new roads and fly-overs face you on return to the Gulf emirate of Dubai and other cities in the United Arab Emirates.

The same picture prevails in most other Gulf Arab oil states, which are still in the grip of a construction fever -- although on a smaller scale than the one that followed the 1991 Gulf War or the building frenzy of the 1970s oil boom.
The industry is a leading non-oil sector contributor to the Gulf economies and an important employer.
"There is an endless thirst for new buildings, shopping malls and houses," one Saudi Arabian industry executive said.
"Cement prices are among the cheapest in the world, labour from the subcontinent is cheap and Gulf Arabs are generally wealthy and like to invest in different sectors," he said.

Industry analysts say the pace of growth has slowed since the early 1990s, but new buildings, roads and industrial plant are still mushrooming across the region, where the population is growing at around three to four percent annually.

They say the oil-dependent economies of the Gulf Arab states -- Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates -- are developing economies that still need billions of dollars in infrastructure development.

Officials say the six states need to spend about $40 billion in the next decade on infrastructure ranging from ports, roads, power stations, water desalination plants, schools and homes to huge petrochemical plants.

But unlike the oil boom heyday of the 1970s and despite a recent surge in oil prices, the private sector will have to meet some of the cost. Governments, hurt by huge Gulf War costs and low oil prices that have rebounded only this year, are tightening their belts to eliminate huge budget deficits.
"After the Gulf War, construction turned into a stable and growing industry that is witnessing more private sector involvement as well as innovative financing," an economist said.
Contractors say some Gulf governments are delaying projects and payments, but many remained upbeat about business prospects.
"They are wealthy developing countries and we don't see any shortage in projects for the foreseeable future," one said.

"People say the industry is stagnant now...But that is not true, it is growing. After the Gulf War there was a pent-up demand. People planning any building in 1990 and 1991 postponed that, so there was a backlog. Now it is steady," another said.
In Saudi Arabia, the biggest Gulf economy, construction contributed 13 percent to non-oil gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1990-95 period.

"In the past the government has been a major source of demand for the construction industry...during the sixth development plan the private sector is expected to become more efficient in the implementation of planned construction projects," it said in its five-year development plan to 2000.

"Output of the construction sector is targeted to grow at an average annual rate of 4.0 percent in the sixth plan, and employment in the sector will continue to account for around 15 to 16 percent of total employment," it said.

In the UAE, where construction contributes about 10 percent to GDP, industry sources said the $4 billion industry was maintaining its momentum. They said the exodus of nearly 150,000 illegal workers, most of them construction labour, under tough new laws would affect the industry only in the short term.
Kuwait witnessed the Gulf's biggest boom after the war to replace infrastructure damaged by the Iraqi occupiers. Business is still good, but analysts say it is no longer state-driven.
Bahrain, the least wealthy of the six, said recently it had an ambitious $2.39 billion plan to upgrade its infrastructure.
In Qatar, whose North Field is the world's single largest gas field, contractors say business is booming.

"North Field development has generated a construction boom...Major companies are busy with jobs created by North Field projects and medium and small companies are full to capacity with other less specialised projects like roads and buildings," said Khaled Abu Baker, general manager of al-Haya Contracting.
Oman has various infrastructure projects in the pipeline, the biggest of which is a $6 billion scheme to produce 6.6 million tonnes a year of liquefied natural gas from the year 2000.

Most of the 22 cement producers in the six states have embarked on ambitious expansion projects to bring supply and demand closer. Industry analysts say this is the best indication of a rapidly growing construction industry.
